Principles of laparoscopic surgery isn't in this year's lecture list — only its gift file exists, so this page is built from every gift (red), grouped by topic, with short added background boxes. There are no slides, notes or Aldughaither chapter.

1. Advantages, indications & contraindications

Added explanationWhy laparoscopy: smaller wounds → less pain, less wound infection and hernia, faster recovery and shorter stay, and a smaller metabolic (stress) response. Contraindications: patient can't tolerate pneumoperitoneum (severe cardiopulmonary disease), uncorrected coagulopathy, and no safe access — a "frozen" abdomen from dense adhesions. Ascites or metastases alone don't forbid it.
  • True about laparoscopy → a frozen abdomen is a contraindication. 439 ×3
  • Palliative operation, bowel adhered together — why not laparoscopy → contraindicated when there is no safe access. 439 ×3
  • Right hemicolectomy — what reduces the metabolic response → laparoscopic approach. 438 ×4

2. Pneumoperitoneum

Added explanationCO₂ is used because it is non-flammable, cheap and widely available, colourless, and highly soluble in blood (rapidly absorbed and exhaled, so a gas embolus is less dangerous). Oxygen and nitrous oxide support combustion with diathermy; air embolizes. Pressure: 12–15 mmHg in adults (≈ 12 is the usual pre-set). Access by a Veress needle (closed) or Hasson open technique; start with low flow (~1–2 L/min) through the Veress needle and increase once in. Veress needles come in lengths of about 80–150 mm.
  • Why carbon dioxide → cheap and available in large amounts. 438 ×5
  • Why carbon dioxide → non-toxic, inert and easily soluble. 437
  • Gas runs out and a colleague suggests the oxygen tank → "Sorry, it is not safe." 435
  • Pressure to maintain for pneumoperitoneum → 12 mmHg. 439 ×2 439 ×2
  • Instrument used to insufflate gas to create the space → Veress needle. 438 ×4
  • Maximum flow rate through a Veress needle → 2 L/min. 438
  • Veress needle size not available → 40 cm. 438
Added explanationThe insufflator shows (left to right) the gas-supply (cylinder) indicator, the intra-abdominal pressure (actual vs set, mmHg), the flow rate (L/min) and the total volume of gas used (L).
  • Insufflator screens (picture) — correct statement → screen 2 shows the pressure inside the abdomen. 438 ×2

3. Equipment

Added explanationThe laparoscopic tower has three pillars: gas insufflator, light source, and camera head with monitor (plus a recorder and energy device). Trocars: sharp bladed (cutting) tips are the most dangerous; blunt/bladeless (conical or optical) trocars are safest. Energy devices: the Harmonic scalpel is ultrasonic (vibrating blade); LigaSure is advanced bipolar vessel sealing. Staple cartridge colours code the staple leg (closed height) length for different tissue thickness (white 2.5 mm thin/vascular → blue 3.5 → gold 3.8–4.2 → green 4.8 → black 5 mm thick tissue).
  • Main pillars of the laparoscopic tower → gas insufflator, light source, and camera head with monitor. 438 ×4
  • Tower picture with numbered units → number 4: light source. 438
  • Safest trocar among four tips (picture) → pic 3 (blunt, bladeless). 435
  • Device in the picture → vessel sealing system. 438
  • Harmonic scalpel vs LigaSure → Harmonic is ultrasonic; LigaSure is bipolar. 435
  • Stapler colours (blue, white, green, black…) determine → length of the staple leg. 438 ×2

4. Set-up & NOTES

Added explanationThe monitor faces the surgeon, in line with the target organ: for an appendectomy the surgeon stands on the patient's left and the monitor goes on the patient's right (for a cholecystectomy, at the right shoulder). NOTES = natural orifice transluminal endoscopic surgery — reaching the peritoneal cavity through a natural orifice (transgastric, transvaginal, transrectal, transvesical) with no skin incision.
  • Monitor position for laparoscopic appendectomy → right side of the patient. 438
  • NOTES stands for → natural orifice transluminal endoscopic surgery. 438
  • Natural-orifice access route among the options → transrectal. 435

5. After laparoscopic surgery

  • Day-case lap cholecystectomy — what to assess on the ward → cardio-respiratory assessment. 434 ×4
  • Diabetic hypertensive man after laparoscopic hernia repair under GA — specifically monitor → myocardial infarction. 438 ×6
